The macroscale level of the air analysis for vehicular emissions of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen indicates little difference in future total pollutant burden whether the project is built or not built.
It appears from the gross aircraft emissions study that aircraft emissions are the predominant source of carbon monoxide in the immediate vicinity of the airport. Although aircraft emissions at General "itchell Field are expected to remain about the same for the next few years, background levels as measured at the air terminal and used in the microscale analysis do not exceed the federal air quality standards.
The most important determination of the air quality analysis consists of comparing the predicted pollution levels and existing or background levels with the National Ambient Air Quality Standards. These federal air quality standards are presented in figure 24 and have been established with an adequate margin of safety to protect the public health and welfare. The standards reflect the maximum allowable concentration of a pollutant not to be exceeded more than once a year.
The microscale analysis consisted of predicting carbon monoxide concentration levels within the vicinity of six selected receptor sites for the years 1977 and 1990. These levels were calculated for both the build and no build conditions leading to the worst probable impact. The receptor locations were selected as sites most directly affected by vehicular traffic on the proposed Airport Spur and on the major connecting roadways where traffic volumes are forecasted to increase as a result of the proposed project. See figure 25 for the location of the sensitive air quality receptors analyzed in the study.
